_doc: Every control M3 ships, and for each one THE TEST THAT WOULD FAIL if the
thing it guards were completely broken (M3 task 3.6).
WHY THIS EXISTS. The constitution asks of every control: if the thing this
guards were completely broken, would this go red? Nine controls have failed
that question in two weeks. Answering it by asserting 'yes' is worth
nothing, so this register answers it by NAMING the test, and the
planted-failure harness then BREAKS each control and requires that exact
test to go red.
A control nobody has watched fail is a control nobody should trust.
HOW IT IS USED:
per PR   control-register.test.ts checks every entry points at a test
that exists, and prints the boundary report.
per PR   the planted-failure harness runs AUTOMATICALLY when the PR
touches any test file named here, because the author of a
desensitising change is the person who still has the context.
nightly  the harness runs over every entry.
on call  workflow_dispatch, for when somebody wants it now.
planted.kind is 'source' (a find/replace in a file) or 'sql' (statements
against the ephemeral branch). Either way the harness asserts the mutation
TOOK EFFECT before running the test, because a harness that silently stops
mutating would report every control as correctly red while doing nothing.
WHY AN ENTRY STAYS EVEN WHEN SOMETHING ELSE WOULD CATCH IT (ruled 17 Aug
2026). The test applied to each entry is: would its absence be noticed by
something else? A control another control already catches does not need its
own entry; one that nothing else would notice needs one badly.
But COVERAGE THAT IS INCIDENTAL IS NOT COVERAGE THAT IS DESIGNED. The
channel-gate-column entry looked redundant because a behavioural break in
mayReachMember also shows up in the phone-rules suite. That overlap is an
accident of how those tests happen to be written: narrow the fixtures or
refactor the suite and the coverage vanishes with nobody noticing, because
nothing wrote down that it was guarding rule 3's behavioural half. An entry
whose absence is only noticed by accident is exactly the one worth keeping.
The register exists to make coverage EXPLICIT rather than EMERGENT.
A near-miss is also kept: invitation-token-prefix's absence IS noticed, but
as the wrong problem. The consumer refuses the value and the failure reads as
a bug in redemption rather than in minting, and 'noticed as the wrong
problem' is close enough to not noticed.
OWED ENTRIES (status: owed). A control that is DESIGNED but not yet BUILT
gets an entry naming the test it owes, rather than being omitted until it
exists. An enumeration that silently omits what is not built is how three
unguarded things arrive later, which is the SENSITIVE_ACTIONS precedent:
unbuilt actions carry built:false and a test asserts each has NO route, so
building one without flipping the flag fails.
Here the same shape: an owed entry's named test must NOT yet exist. Writing
it without clearing the status fails, which sends the author to the entry
where the planted failure and the reasoning are already written.
CLEARING  FORCES THE HARNESS TO RUN. owed is an EXEMPTION: this file
skips the name check for those entries and the harness skips them entirely.
Clearing the status is a CLAIM THAT THE CONTROL NOW EXISTS, and the register
must not accept that claim without the proof it exists for.
An exemption that expires without anything checking AT THE MOMENT IT EXPIRES
is an exemption that outlives its reason, which is the same shape as a trigger
tied to a module number: the thing that made it safe stops being true and
nothing notices. CI diffs this file against the base and treats any entry that
left owed as a touched test, so the mutation runs even when the test file
itself is unchanged.

planted.apply: ALTER TABLE invitations DROP CONSTRAINT invitations_token_purpose_prefix
planted.restore: DELETE FROM invitations WHERE token NOT LIKE 'ms\_invite\_%'; ALTER TABLE invitations ADD CONSTRAINT invitations_token_purpose_prefix CHECK (token LIKE 'ms\_invite\_%')

planted.restoreNote: The mutation lets the named test insert a row the constraint forbids, so the restore must remove it first. Found by running the harness: the restore failed with 'is violated by some row', which is a flaw in the planted failure rather than in the control.

planted.restore: REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION public.auth_household_id(text) FROM marginsheet_sync

A planted failure that does not actually break the control tests the harness, not the control.

controls.guards: Two members of one household see each other; other households do not.
controls.name: THE TWO-MEMBER ASSERTION: the household is the unit

planted.apply: ALTER POLICY household_isolation ON members USING (household_id = nullif(btrim(current_setting('marginsheet.household_id', true)), '')::uuid AND is_primary)
planted.restore: ALTER POLICY household_isolation ON members USING (household_id = nullif(btrim(current_setting('marginsheet.household_id', true)), '')::uuid)
planted.proof: select (pg_get_expr(polqual, polrelid) like '%is_primary%')::int as n from pg_policy p join pg_class c on c.oid = p.polrelid where c.relname = 'members' and p.polname = 'household_isolation'
planted.note: SUBTLY WRONG IN ONE DIRECTION, not off. An earlier version used USING (false), which proves the test fails when the policy is disabled, and the control is not guarding against disabled: off breaks loudly for everyone immediately and nobody would miss it. What it guards against is the policy being scoped PER MEMBER rather than per household, which is exactly the wrong direction that passed every isolation test for two weeks. This narrows visibility to a single member of the household while leaving cross-household isolation intact, so only the two-member assertion can detect it. Ruled by Guy, 17 Aug 2026: if this does not redden the test, the test is not proving what the register says it proves.

controls.guards: The Plaid sync worker cannot read a household's conversation, memory or advisory record.
controls.name: is REFUSED a read of

planted.apply: GRANT SELECT ON messages TO marginsheet_sync
planted.restore: REVOKE ALL ON messages FROM marginsheet_sync
planted.note: THE DIRECTION IS THE POINT. Re-granting one forbidden table reproduces exactly the pre-0023 state: the role stays able to do its job, every pipeline test still passes, and nothing anywhere is visibly broken. That is the failure this control exists to catch, and it is the failure that sat in the schema for two weeks. Revoking a table the role NEEDS would also redden a test, and would prove almost nothing, because a sync worker that cannot read plaid_items breaks loudly on its first run. THE PROOF ASSERTS THE STATE IT FOUND RATHER THAN THE ABSENCE OF WHAT IT DID, after 20 Aug 2026. REVOKE ALL is deliberately broader than the plant, which is safe only while 0023 leaves this role nothing on this table, and the old proof asked about SELECT alone so it could not have noticed the restore removing a privilege the plant never granted. It now sums SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE into one number, so restored must read 0: not 'the thing I did is gone' but 'the table is as I found it'.

controls.distinction: Asserts 42501 rather than row counts. Every forbidden table carries household_isolation, so a read this role IS permitted returns zero rows when no GUC is set: a test asserting 'nothing came back' would pass with the wide grant fully intact, proving RLS works and saying nothing about the grant.
controls.nameNote: A SUBSTRING, deliberately. The three forbidden-table tests are generated in a loop, so no full title appears literally in the source and the register's existence check could not find one. vitest -t matches substrings, so this runs all three; the planted failure reddens one of them and the run fails, which is what the harness reads. Caught by the register check itself, which exists precisely to stop a -t filter that matches nothing being read as a pass.

controls.guards: An eleventh table granted to the sync role is noticed, even when nobody named it.
controls.name: holds grants on exactly the 10 tables

planted.apply: GRANT SELECT ON receivables TO marginsheet_sync
planted.restore: REVOKE ALL ON receivables FROM marginsheet_sync
planted.note: A table NOBODY NAMED, deliberately. sync-role-boundary attempts messages, known_context and decision_journal and requires three refusals, and all three still pass when a fourth table is granted. receivables is in none of those lists, so only the count notices. That is why this entry exists separately from sync-role-boundary. THE PROOF ASSERTS THE STATE IT FOUND RATHER THAN THE ABSENCE OF WHAT IT DID, after 20 Aug 2026. REVOKE ALL is deliberately broader than the plant, which is safe only while 0023 leaves this role nothing on this table, and the old proof asked about SELECT alone so it could not have noticed the restore removing a privilege the plant never granted. It now sums SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE into one number, so restored must read 0: not 'the thing I did is gone' but 'the table is as I found it'.

controls.distinction: A COUNT CATCHES A WIDENING A NAMED-ITEM CHECK CANNOT. sync-role-boundary proves three specific tables are refused; this proves the set is exactly nine. Grant a fourth table nobody thought to name and the three refusals still pass while the count goes to ten. The deployed Worker reports the same number independently: sync/health returns tables:9 from information_schema, which only shows tables the connecting role holds privilege on, against api's 46. WIDENED DELIBERATELY 18 Aug 2026, nine to ten, for the household-state-changed outbox. A control firing on a legitimate widening is the control working, and the declaration moved BEFORE the grant so the red was a proof rather than a description. The reasoning that admits the tenth is narrow ON PURPOSE, because it is what stops an eleventh being argued in by analogy: the sync worker must write the signal inside the same transaction as the change it describes, so a write by anything else loses the atomicity the outbox exists for. Not 'the pipeline touches it'.

controls.guards: A tampered ciphertext cannot be decrypted into something a caller treats as a token.
controls.name: rejects a single flipped byte of ciphertext, under the correct key

planted.find: throw new Error("decryption failed: wrong key or tampered ciphertext");
planted.note: SWALLOWS THE FAILURE instead of raising, which is the shape that ships: a caller receives an empty string where it expected a token and carries on. The first version switched AES-GCM to AES-CTR and was INERT: the key is imported for AES-GCM, so the mismatched algorithm threw anyway and the test could not tell why. Found by running the harness after it was fixed to resolve the owning package.

controls.distinction: The wrong-key test is NOT this control. A wrong key can be refused upstream of authentication, by importKey's length check or the base64 check, so it passes whether or not the tag is verified. Only a flipped ciphertext byte under the correct key isolates the tag.

controls.guards: A failed Plaid call cannot leak the access token into a log, a Sentry payload or a serialised error.
controls.name: throws without the token when the TRANSPORT fails

planted.replace: throw new Error(`Plaid ${endpoint} failed after sending ${body}`);
planted.note: PUTS THE REQUEST BODY IN THE MESSAGE, which is the postgres incident's exact shape and what a wrapper adding context actually does. The first version stashed `cause` on globalThis and was INERT: the thrown error never carried it, so nothing the test inspects changed.

controls.distinction: Amended 18 Aug 2026 from Plaid's RESPONSE shape to our REQUEST envelope. Seven Plaid error classes captured from Sandbox return an identical seven-key envelope with no request echo, so a scrubber aimed at Plaid's errors would pass forever guarding nothing. The token is in the request.

controls.guards: The leak probe's coverage stays total rather than becoming partial when somebody adds a second call site.
controls.name: finds Plaid request construction in exactly one place

planted.note: ADDS A SECOND CALL SITE RATHER THAN BREAKING THE SCANNER (Guy, 18 Aug 2026). A broken scanner is a defect somebody notices; a second call site in services/api is the thing that could genuinely happen in M5 or M13, and it makes the leak probe's coverage partial while every test stays green. Breaking the scanner would redden the test and prove only that the scanner runs.

controls.distinction: This is the coverage-degenerate failure rather than a control failure. token-never-escapes guards one module and nothing else enforced that the module was the only one. Direction 2 of this test binds the pair together: it asserts the probe imports from the module this scan names, so a rename cannot empty either.

controls.guards: Balance drift beyond tolerance is noticed rather than absorbed.
controls.name: drift beyond tolerance opens an investigation item

planted.note: Widening the tolerance to infinity. Owed with the control at 4.6.

controls.distinction: Registered BEFORE it is built, deliberately. An enumeration that silently omits what is not built is how unguarded things arrive later: the precedent is SENSITIVE_ACTIONS, where three unbuilt actions carry built:false and a test asserts each has no route. Proves only that the test notices a DISABLED tolerance; the blocking half is a separate entry.

controls.control: the block on a drifting account's numbers
controls.guards: No customer-visible number ships from an account with an open drift investigation.
controls.name: an account with an open investigation ships no numbers

planted.note: Tolerance INTACT, the block removed. Owed with the control at 4.6.

controls.distinction: THE ONE THAT MATTERS, and the reason these are two entries. If blocking broke, would the detection test notice? No: drift is still detected, the investigation item still opens, the test still passes, and the number ships anyway. That is what Base44 had. A reconciliation check that reports without blocking looks healthy from every angle.

controls.guards: No access token crosses the service binding back into the Worker with public routes.
controls.name: no serialisation of the REAL result contains the token

planted.note: RETURNS THE TOKEN FROM THE REAL HANDLER, which is how this would actually happen: somebody needs it downstream and adds a field. Verified 18 Aug 2026: both leak assertions go red, the two structural assertions stay green, everything green on restore. The entry was REMOVED on 18 Aug when the harness showed the old test asserted a hand-written literal and could not fail; it returns now that the test calls the real function.

controls.distinction: Asserted by ENUMERATION on the real return value rather than by scanning for token-shaped strings. A scan only knows the prefixes it was taught, so a field carrying the token under another name passes it; the enumeration fails on any field that was not there before, which is the actual failure mode. The token demonstrably ENTERS the function under test, so this proves it did not leave rather than that it was never present.

controls.control: reconnect's lookup and status update (M4 task 4.3.4)
controls.guards: Repairing one login at a bank does not orphan the household's other login at the same bank.
controls.name: leaves the OTHER Item at the same institution untouched

planted.note: WIDENS THE UPDATE from one Item to every Item the household owns, which is the shape of keying on anything but the Item. Verified 18 Aug 2026: both orphaning assertions go red, the three structural assertions stay green, all green on restore.

controls.distinction: THE ASSERTION IS ON THE ITEM NOBODY ASKED ABOUT. From the reconnected Item's side, a correct reconnect and one keyed on the institution are IDENTICAL: it returns healthy, updated and syncing in both worlds. Only the other Item shows the difference. The other Item also starts BROKEN in the fixture, because an earlier version left it healthy and asserted it was still healthy, where the expected value and the wrong value were the same string.

controls.control: the repair sweep's enqueued_at predicate (M4 task 4.4.5)
controls.guards: The repair sweep cannot become a poller for unannounced work.
controls.name: does not return a row that was never announced

planted.find:
where enqueued_at is not null
       and claimed_at is null
planted.note: DROPS THE enqueued_at CLAUSE, which is exactly the change that turns the sweep into a poller. It would still work, still repair dropped notifications, and additionally pick up work no notification ever announced. Verified 18 Aug 2026: three tests redden, including the partition assertion, and the COUNTER's tests stay green, which is the discrimination that matters.

controls.distinction: A comment claiming 'this is not polling' is the section 514 shape: a sentence that reads as a constraint and enforces nothing. This control makes the difference CHECKABLE. Paired with counter-sees-unannounced-rows, which points the opposite way at the same column.

controls.guards: A crash in the commit-to-enqueue window is observable rather than silent.
controls.name: counts the never-announced row

planted.find:
where enqueued_at is null
       and created_at <
planted.replace:
where enqueued_at is not null
       and created_at <
planted.note: INVERTS THE COUNTER so it looks at announced rows. It then reads zero forever and ITS SILENCE MEANS NOTHING, which is indistinguishable from the window never being hit. Verified 18 Aug 2026: three tests redden and the SWEEP's tests stay green.

controls.distinction: THE OPPOSITE DIRECTION FROM sweep-is-blind-to-unannounced-rows, ON THE SAME COLUMN. The sweep must not see unannounced rows; the counter must. Together they make the sweep's blindness deliberate rather than accidental: a blindness with nothing watching it is a loss nobody can observe, and a counter without a blind sweep is just a poller in two parts. If the window is truly a millisecond the counter reads zero forever AND ITS SILENCE MEANS SOMETHING.

controls.guards: A refused pagination is not retried from the cursor Plaid refused, which would replay transactions into a household's ledger.
controls.name: restarts from LAST COMPLETED, never from the refused in-flight cursor

planted.note: RETRIES THE REFUSED CURSOR, which is the change a well-meaning person makes: the sync failed, so retry it. Verified 18 Aug 2026, exactly one test reddens and it is the one naming the replay. The loop still terminates, still completes, still reports sensible counts. Nothing else notices, which is the criterion for its own entry.

controls.distinction: The failure this guards is not a crash. Retrying the in-flight cursor SUCCEEDS and produces duplicate transactions in a household's ledger, arriving through a change that looked like reliability work and had a green suite behind it. Tested against a SYNTHESISED 400: the real error reproduced 3 times in 5 against Sandbox, which is flaky and therefore not a fixture, so this proves our handler takes the right branch and does not claim to have proven Plaid's behaviour.

controls.guards: A long backfill making steady progress is not swept as stuck.
controls.name: does NOT sweep a four-hour backfill that wrote a cursor a minute ago

planted.note: MEASURES FROM SYNC START, which is the implementation somebody naturally writes: the question sounds like 'has this been running too long'. Verified 18 Aug 2026, three tests redden including BOTH DIRECTIONS, the healthy long backfill and the recently-started dead sync.

controls.distinction: The fixture's failure case is a HEALTHY long backfill, and it has to exist among the values the fixture can take or nothing is proven: a suite whose syncs all start recently cannot distinguish measuring from progress from measuring from start, because both answer the same for a short sync. The damage is also not a crash. Measured from start, a large first backfill is swept mid-flight, set back to queued, restarted and swept again, so an Item working perfectly NEVER FINISHES while every status looks busy.

controls.guards: A transaction Plaid stops reporting is flagged, not erased from the household's books.
controls.name: issues an update and no delete

planted.find:
update transactions
       set removed = true, updated_at = now()
     where
planted.note: DELETES INSTEAD OF FLAGGING, which is the obvious reading of 'removed' and what somebody writes without the spec open. Verified 18 Aug 2026: two tests redden.

controls.distinction: A DELETE loses a row nobody can reconstruct, and the household sees a month's Kept figure change with no record of why. It is also irreversible in a way the flag is not: Plaid can report a transaction removed and later report it again, and a flag can be cleared where a deleted row cannot be recovered.

controls.control: the IS NULL guard on first_sync_completed_at (M4 task 4.4.4)
controls.guards: A second sync cannot re-arm the intro trigger and introduce a household to MyKeeper twice.
controls.name: guards on IS NULL in the WHERE clause, not by reading first

planted.find:
where id = ${householdId}
       and first_sync_completed_at is null
planted.note: DROPS THE GUARD. Verified 18 Aug 2026: two tests redden, the structural one and the behavioural one. The behavioural one only catches it because the test stub MODELS the guard rather than returning a flat empty result, which would have passed whether or not the WHERE clause existed.

controls.distinction: The guard is a WHERE clause rather than a read-then-write because a read-then-write RACES: two Items finishing their first sync together both read NULL and both write, and the second moves a timestamp M13's intro trigger and the day-3-to-5 census treat as immutable.

controls.guards: The household an exchange writes into is derived from the session and can never be named by the caller.
controls.name: ignores a householdId in the body and uses the session's household

planted.replace:
// PLANTED: the caller's value wins by key order.
          body: JSON.stringify({ publicToken: body.publicToken, householdId, ...(await request.clone().json() as object) }),
planted.note: THE MUTATION REINTRODUCES THE DEFECT IN ITS MOST PLAUSIBLE FORM, a spread of the caller's body over the derived value, rather than deleting the session lookup. Deleting the lookup breaks loudly and proves only that a test exists; a spread leaves code that READS correct and is the shape somebody writes while 'passing through the rest of the body'. Verified red by CI's planted-failure harness, which provisions a Neon branch this test needs.

controls.distinction: THIS IS NOT A CONTROL THAT GUARDED NOTHING, WHICH IS WHAT EVERY OTHER FINDING THIS WEEK WAS. It is an authorization boundary that was pointed at the attacker: exchange.ts did set_config('marginsheet.household_id', <body value>), so every RLS policy enforced isolation faithfully for whichever household the caller named. RLS cannot help when the household id is the INPUT to the GUC rather than a constraint on it. The 401 assertion is separate from the derivation assertion on purpose: the defect answered 400, because the body was checked and the caller never was, and a 400 reads as malformed rather than as unauthenticated.

controls.guards: No household id is composed into a response, URL, email or client-reachable surface.
controls.name: is composed into no response, URL or message

planted.note: A new endpoint returning a household id, which is the shape that would actually occur: somebody adds a surface, not somebody edits the scanner. Verified red 19 Aug 2026, reporting services/api/src/index.ts and the planted line.

controls.distinction: THIS GUARDS A MITIGATION, NOT A BOUNDARY, AND THAT IS WHY IT EXISTS. The severity of anything taking a household id as input rests on a stranger being unable to obtain one, which was true when traced and was maintained by NOTHING. The first feature to put one in a link would have removed it silently. It scans SOURCE rather than payloads because a household id is a bare UUID with no structure to recognise at runtime. Two false positives on the first run, an internal service-binding forward and an error message naming the field, and THE DETECTOR WAS FIXED RATHER THAN THE CODE: rewriting an error message to satisfy a scanner is the ceremony that teaches people to suppress a rule.

controls.guards: The removed stream cannot flag a transaction belonging to another household, without relying on RLS.
controls.name: scopes the update by household_id, not by plaid_transaction_id alone

planted.note: Removes the household predicate, restoring EXACTLY the statement that was confirmed on 19 Aug 2026 to flag another household's transaction with threw=nothing. The mutation is the historical defect rather than an invented one, which is the strongest form available: the direction of the break is known to occur because it did.

controls.distinction: TASK 4e, AND IT LANDED BEFORE THE AUTHORIZATION FIX ON PURPOSE. The statement must be correct even when the policy is wrong, and the policy IS wrong: sync_worker_access is USING (true) for marginsheet_sync, so RLS scopes nothing on this path and the household GUC is decorative. ORDERING ARGUMENT: 4c must not be verified against code that depends on it. With this correct on its own terms, landing 4c tests whether the narrowing works; landing 4c first would test only whether the narrowing is the one thing standing between us and a known-bad statement. This is a SHAPE assertion over recorded SQL rather than a database test, which is honest about what it proves: it proves the statement names a household, and the database-level proof is the confirmed finding on branch finding/cross-household-upsert.

controls.guards: No write in the sync Worker lacks a household, so 4c's policy cannot refuse a path nobody declared.
controls.name: no write statement is unscoped

planted.note: Restores the one statement the scan actually found on its first run, which is the historical state rather than an invented break. Verified red 19 Aug 2026, naming outbox.ts and the statement.

controls.distinction: STEP 4c-i, LANDED BEFORE THE POLICY AND ON ITS OWN, because setting a household changes nothing while sync_worker_access is still USING (true). That makes the policy the only variable when 4c lands and something breaks (Guy). IT IS A SOURCE SCAN AND SAYS SO: it proves each write names a household or sits in a file that sets the GUC, and it CANNOT prove the GUC is set on the same transaction as the write, which is a runtime property. The database-level proof is 4c-iii's negative controls, which is why this is not sufficient alone. It also carries the fifth write path, which is a HOLE rather than a statement: runTransactionsSync takes persistInFlight as an injected callback, so the cursor write lives in a caller that does not exist, and a scan cannot find a statement that is not there.

controls.guards: The sync role cannot write into another household's row on a table scoped by household_id.
controls.name: an ORDINARY table refuses a write into another household

planted.proof: select count(*)::int from pg_policies where tablename = 'plaid_items' and policyname = 'sync_worker_write' and qual like '%household_id%'
planted.apply: DROP POLICY "sync_worker_write" ON "plaid_items"; CREATE POLICY "sync_worker_write" ON "plaid_items" FOR ALL TO marginsheet_sync USING (true) WITH CHECK (true);
planted.restore: DROP POLICY "sync_worker_write" ON "plaid_items"; CREATE POLICY "sync_worker_write" ON "plaid_items" FOR ALL TO marginsheet_sync USING (household_id = nullif(btrim(current_setting('marginsheet.household_id', true)), '')::uuid) WITH CHECK (household_id = nullif(btrim(current_setting('marginsheet.household_id', true)), '')::uuid);
planted.note: RESTORES USING (true) IN THE DATABASE, which is the historical state that allowed the confirmed write. IT IS A `sql` MUTATION AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT: the first version edited the migration FILE, which is inert, because the branch is migrated before the harness runs and changing an already-applied .sql changes nothing. All three policy controls reported 'broke it yes, went red NO' and the cause was the mutation, not the control.

controls.distinction: ONE OF THREE CONTROLS THAT DIFFER IN KIND. One refusal proves a boundary exists; three of the same shape prove one predicate works three times. This is the ordinary case, where household_id is the scope. Its SURVIVAL assertion is the property rather than the error: a refusal by policy and a match of zero rows are both acceptable, and asserting on the exception message would couple the control to Postgres wording.

controls.guards: An unattributed webhook is writable and an attributed one is scoped.
controls.name: provider_events accepts an UNATTRIBUTED row and refuses another household's

planted.proof: select count(*)::int from pg_policies where tablename = 'provider_events' and policyname = 'sync_worker_write' and qual like '%IS NULL%'

A network failure, a rate limit, an unrecognised error code and a missing token all produce unknown, and under this mutation all four delete the household's rows for an Item that may still be live at Plaid. Nothing about the code looks wrong.

controls.distinction: THE FAILURE THIS GUARDS IS SILENT AND THE ONE IT PREVENTS IS NOT. A duplicate ledger after a relink is visible: Kept and Margin move by the value of the overlap. Deleting rows for a LIVE Item leaves a household connected at Plaid, billed monthly, with no row, no sync and no way to find it except by reading Plaid's dashboard. So the gate is deliberately asymmetric: refusing a purge that should have proceeded costs one manual retry, and permitting one that should not costs an invisible connection. The third assertion checks the GONE set itself, because widening that list would undo the gate without touching the gate's own line.

controls.guards: A confirmed disconnect reads the Item's liveness itself, at the moment of removal, rather than trusting a value read earlier.
controls.name: reads liveness itself rather than accepting it as a parameter

planted.find: const status = await itemStatus(householdId, itemId, credentials, encryptionKey, databaseUrl);
planted.replace: const status = { liveness: "live" as ItemLiveness, detail: { assumed: true } };
planted.note: REPLACES THE FRESH READ WITH AN ASSUMPTION, which is the optimisation somebody would actually reach for: the caller just ran a dry run, the answer was live, and asking again looks like a wasted Plaid call. It type-checks, it reads as a reasonable simplification, and it turns the gate below into a tautology that always passes. Nothing about the resulting code looks wrong.

controls.distinction: THE GATE AND THE FRESHNESS OF WHAT IT GATES ARE TWO DIFFERENT PROPERTIES, and only one of them is visible in the gate's own line. 'refuses a confirmed call unless liveness is live' checks the comparison; this checks that the value being compared was obtained NOW. A dry run minutes earlier is not evidence about the present: an Item can be removed, expire or lose its credential in between. It is the same shape as the household GUC that did not survive between statements, recorded 20 Aug 2026: two individually correct reads with nothing establishing that the first still describes the second. Direction 2 asserts the module still calls /item/remove at all, because a file that stopped removing anything would satisfy a scan looking only for the absence of a parameter.

controls.guards: Every module that opens its own database connection and writes declares the household, so no write policy from 0026 evaluates against an unset setting.
controls.name: is set at all by every file that opens a connection and writes

planted.note: REMOVES THE ONLY DECLARATION FROM THE SYNC RUNNER, which is how disconnect.ts actually shipped: nobody writes a wrong GUC, the failure mode is that nobody writes one at all. The resulting code reads correctly and every statement still names the household in its own WHERE clause; the writes simply stop matching, because 0026's write policies read a SETTING rather than the statement. IT POINTS AT run-sync.ts RATHER THAN AT disconnect.ts, AND THAT IS THE CORRECTION. The first version removed one of TWO calls in disconnect.ts, leaving the other, so the file still contained a declaration and this file-level check stayed green: the harness reported broke-it yes, went-red NO, correctly. It had been verified locally against a strip of BOTH calls, which is a DIFFERENT MUTATION FROM THE ONE REGISTERED. A mutation is verified as written or it is not verified.

controls.distinction: A SCAN THAT CHECKS THE FORM OF WHAT EXISTS CANNOT SEE WHAT IS ABSENT, and this is the second half of a control that had only the first. The receiver scan beside it reads every set_config call and requires a transaction handle, so a file with NO call contributes no rows and passes perfectly. disconnect.ts shipped with an UPDATE and no GUC, sat inside the scanned roots the entire time, and the scan was green. THE DISTINCTION IT DRAWS IS THE WHOLE RULE: a file that opens its own connection owes a GUC, and a helper that receives a tx does not, because the caller declared it. apply-streams.ts and outbox.ts write constantly and correctly set nothing. Direction 2 asserts more than two writing modules were found, because a regex that stopped matching would leave it filtering an empty list and passing.

controls.guards: A removed Item is classified as gone, so the disconnect's repair branch and the purge's gate can ever be reached.
controls.name: says gone for an Item Plaid no longer has

planted.replace:
const shaped = error.toJSON() as { error_code?: string };
    return shaped.error_code && GONE.has(shaped.error_code) ? "gone" : "unknown";
planted.note: RESTORES THE EXACT CODE THAT SHIPPED, which is the strongest available mutation: not a plausible invention but the real one. toJSON emits errorCode and this reads error_code, so the property is always undefined and the classifier can never say gone. IT TYPE-CHECKS, because a cast asserts a shape the compiler then stops verifying, which is why review passed it. Nothing errors at runtime either: every refusal simply reads as caution.

controls.distinction: THE FIRST ASSERTION IS THE ONE THAT WAS MISSING, and its absence is the whole story. Every negative case here would pass against a classifier hard-wired to "unknown", which is precisely what shipped: a function whose refusals all look deliberate. A gate that can only refuse is indistinguishable from a careful gate until something needs it to permit. The consequences were two branches that could never be reached: the disconnect's repair path and the purge's permission to delete. FOUND BECAUSE THE INTERPRETATION TRAVELS WITH ITS EVIDENCE: the reply said liveness unknown while the detail beside it said ITEM_NOT_FOUND, and the contradiction was visible without reading the source.

controls.guards: Two balance writes on one day converge on the later figure in one snapshot rather than accumulating a row per sync.
controls.name: converges on the later figure within a day rather than accumulating

planted.note: KEEPS THE FIRST FIGURE INSTEAD OF THE LAST, which is the plausible wrong version rather than an obvious break: DO NOTHING reads as idempotent and safe, it still writes exactly one row per day so the count assertion passes, and only the VALUE is wrong. A projection reading the series would then see the balance at whatever moment the day's first sync happened to run rather than the closing figure.

controls.distinction: THE PER-DAY CADENCE IS A RULING, NOT AN IMPLEMENTATION DETAIL, which is why it has a control. account_balance_snapshots is keyed by date and the projection reads a SERIES, so a row per sync would make that series depend on how often we happened to sync: a property of us rather than of the household's money. The fixture writes twice within a single day with DISTINCT figures, so accumulating leaves two rows and keeping the first leaves 500.25, and neither can be confused with the correct outcome.
